Threat.value: Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame
I feel threatened by strangers approaching me even in ordinary situations
Unusual silence makes me feel something dangerous is about to happen

Memory.value: Some moments of the event are extremely clear while others are completely blank
Fragments of the memory appear suddenly without warning and then disappear
I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it

Negative Appraisals.value: My life has been destroyed by the trauma
I have to be on guard all the time

issues.explanation: 'Shouting in Arabic' is hard to reconcile with the validated trauma type of stalking unless there is specific trauma detail indicating the stalker used Arabic; with the rest of the profile, this trigger appears overly specific and disconnected from the other stalking-related items.

issues.item: Memory: Verbal Access: I can talk about what happened very easily.
issues.explanation: 'I can talk about what happened very easily' conflicts with the same Memory node items describing fragmented, intrusive, partially inaccessible trauma memory ('extremely clear while others are completely blank' and 'fragments appear suddenly without warning'). While not impossible, this is a direct enough tension within the node to question coherence.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Fear of Rage: I will not be able to control my anger and will do something terrible
issues.explanation: Fear of losing control of anger and doing something terrible is poorly integrated with the rest of the profile, which centers on fear, mistrust, stranger threat, and life damage after stalking. It points toward a perpetration/harm-to-others concern not otherwise represented in Threat, Triggers, Memory, or strategies, making the formulation less coherent.

vignette:
For the past eight months, Sarah has felt like a ghost in her own life, a sentry perpetually on duty in a world that has become a landscape of potential threats. The stalking began subtly, a man she didn't know appearing at the coffee shop she frequented, then later, standing across the street from the elementary school where she teaches. It escalated over three terrifying months. He learned her schedule, her route home, her friends' names. The police were involved, reports were filed, but his presence felt more constant than theirs. The sight of a police car now does little to reassure her; instead, it serves as a stark, uniformed reminder of a time when she was desperately in need of protection and felt she received none. The most visceral memories are auditory. He would call her apartment from a blocked number and say nothing, his presence conveyed only by the sound of his slow, heavy breathing on the other end of the line.

Now, in the quiet of her own home, silence is no longer peaceful. It is a vacuum, a holding of breath before something terrible happens. She keeps the television on constantly, a low murmur of noise to fill the void. This is especially true at night, when the memory of those phone calls is most potent. Fragments of that time surface without warning. While reading a picture book to her first-grade class, the image of his face, seen through her peephole, can flash into her mind with sickening clarity, only to vanish a second later. These moments are islands of terrifying detail in a fog of what she can't-or won't-fully recall. When her partner, Mark, gently asks her what she is thinking, she finds she knows what happened but is unable to give it form. The words simply are not there, leaving her feeling isolated in an experience she cannot share.

Her work, once a source of joy, has become a minefield. As a teacher, she is constantly meeting new people, and she has come to believe that any stranger could harbor a hidden malevolence. A new father dropping off his child, a delivery person at the school's front office-each one is a potential threat to be assessed. She scans their hands, their eyes, their posture, convinced that she must remain on guard at all times to prevent another catastrophe. This constant vigilance is exhausting, leaving her drained and irritable. She no longer walks the few blocks from the bus stop to her apartment, certain that the feeling of footsteps behind her is not paranoia but a reality she has yet to confirm. The extra cost of taxis is a small price to pay for a few minutes of perceived safety.

This deep-seated mistrust has poisoned her relationships. She finds herself questioning Mark's whereabouts, needing to know his exact location to quiet a frantic part of her brain that insists people cannot be trusted. She knows this is unfair, that he is her greatest support, but the belief is as persistent and invasive as the memories themselves. She feels as though her life, the one she was building, has been irrevocably destroyed. Having strong feelings of fear or even anger now feels dangerous in itself, a sign that she is losing control and might shatter completely. It was after a week of barely speaking to Mark, retreating into a silent state of high alert, that he finally told her, "I feel like I'm living with a stranger." The words landed with the weight of truth, prompting her to seek therapy. Sarah is here now because she is terrified that this guarded, frightened version of herself is all that is left, but she holds onto a desperate hope that she might one day feel safe in a quiet room again.
